title: VPS & Nginx
subtitle: Own your server — DigitalOcean/Hetzner VPS, Nginx reverse proxy, PM2 process management, and UFW firewall

content.text: A VPS (Virtual Private Server) is a Linux VM you fully control. You install whatever you want, run any language, and it never sleeps. It's the bottom of the infrastructure ladder — more work than Railway, less complexity than AWS. Hetzner offers 2 vCPU / 4GB RAM VPS for €4.51/month (Europe datacenter). DigitalOcean's equivalent is $12/month. For apps that have outgrown free tiers or need always-on uptime without paying AWS prices, a VPS is the sweet spot.

content.filename: First 5 minutes on a new VPS
content.code:
# After creating VPS (Ubuntu 22.04), SSH in as root:
ssh root@YOUR_SERVER_IP

# 1. Update everything
apt update && apt upgrade -y

# 2. Create a non-root user
adduser deploy
usermod -aG sudo deploy

# 3. Copy SSH key to new user
mkdir /home/deploy/.ssh
cp ~/.ssh/authorized_keys /home/deploy/.ssh/
chown -R deploy:deploy /home/deploy/.ssh
chmod 700 /home/deploy/.ssh
chmod 600 /home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys

# 4. Disable root login and password auth
nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config
# Set: PermitRootLogin no
# Set: PasswordAuthentication no
systemctl restart ssh

# Now SSH as deploy user:
ssh deploy@YOUR_SERVER_IP

# 5. Install Node.js (via nvm)
curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.40.0/install.sh | bash
source ~/.bashrc
nvm install --lts
node --version  # v22.x.x

# 6. Install PM2 globally
npm install -g pm2

# UFW is Ubuntu's simplified iptables interface

# Install
sudo apt install ufw

# Default: deny incoming, allow outgoing
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing

# Allow SSH (CRITICAL — do this before enabling!)
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH
# Or by port:
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp

# Allow HTTP and HTTPS
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp

# Enable UFW (blocks everything except what you allowed)
sudo ufw enable

# Check status
sudo ufw status verbose

# IMPORTANT: Never block port 22 before SSH is allowed
# If you lock yourself out, use the VPS provider's web console

# Your Node.js app runs on port 3000 — don't expose it directly
# Nginx will proxy from port 80/443 → 3000
# So do NOT run: ufw allow 3000

content.filename: Install Nginx and configure reverse proxy
content.code:
# Install Nginx
sudo apt install nginx
sudo systemctl enable nginx
sudo systemctl start nginx

# Create a site configuration
sudo nano /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp

# --- paste the configuration below ---

# Enable the site
sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/

# Remove default site
sudo rm /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default

# Test config syntax
sudo nginx -t

# Reload Nginx
sudo systemctl reload nginx

# Deploy app
cd /home/deploy/myapp
npm ci --production
npm run build

# Start with PM2 (auto-restarts on crash)
pm2 start npm --name myapp -- start

# Or use an ecosystem file for full control:
# pm2 start ecosystem.config.js

# Persist across reboots
pm2 startup  # generates a systemd command — run it
pm2 save     # saves the current process list

# Common PM2 commands:
pm2 status          # list all processes
pm2 logs myapp      # tail logs
pm2 logs myapp --lines 100  # last 100 lines
pm2 restart myapp   # restart
pm2 reload myapp    # zero-downtime reload (for web apps)
pm2 stop myapp      # stop
pm2 delete myapp    # remove from PM2
pm2 monit           # interactive dashboard

content.text: Use pm2 reload instead of pm2 restart in production. restart kills all processes then starts fresh — there's a brief downtime window. reload starts new workers before killing old ones (zero-downtime rolling reload). In cluster mode, PM2 keeps at least one worker alive the entire time. reload is safe to run during a deploy without any user impact.

questions.question: Your Node.js app runs on port 3000 but users access port 443 (HTTPS). In the setup above, what handles this translation?
options: Node.js listens on both port 3000 and port 443
Nginx listens on ports 80 and 443, then proxies requests to 127.0.0.1:3000 (your app)
The domain DNS record includes the port number
questions.explanation: Nginx is the reverse proxy. It listens on public ports 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS), handles SSL termination, then forwards requests to your Node.js app running on localhost:3000 — which never needs to handle SSL or be exposed to the internet. This is a standard pattern: Nginx handles the public-facing concerns (SSL, headers, static files, rate limiting), while your app focuses on business logic. Port 3000 is only accessible from within the server itself (127.0.0.1), not from the internet.

faq.q: How do I deploy updates to my VPS?
faq.a: The most common approach for a solo dev: SSH in, git pull, npm ci, npm run build, pm2 reload myapp. For teams, use GitHub Actions: SSH to your server from CI using a stored SSH key, run the same commands. For a more automated approach, tools like Kamal (used by Basecamp) or Deployer handle this workflow with rollback support.

examples: Thousands of bootstrapped SaaS companies run on Hetzner or DigitalOcean VPS with exactly this stack. A €4.51/month Hetzner VPS can comfortably serve 500,000+ requests/day for a typical Node.js API — the economics are dramatically better than managed PaaS at scale
Many companies that started on Heroku (now expensive) migrated to this exact setup: VPS + Nginx + PM2. The migration takes a day and can cut monthly bills by 80%
